name: Reseda
lede: Reseda is a pale green named for the mignonette flower, and the Latin name behind it also belongs to weld, the plant that was Europe's main yellow dye from antiquity to the nineteenth century.

sections.title: A flower, and a family of plants
sections.body:
Paterson defines *reseda* as a light-green or grey-green color taken from the mignonette plant, and defines mignonette as the greyish green of its flower, similar to reseda [1]. The mignonette is *Reseda odorata*, named by Linnaeus; a flower book of 1851 says it came to Europe from Egypt in 1750 and reached England in 1752 [2]. The same book says the Latin *resedo* means to calm, and that the plants were once laid on bruises to ease pain [2]. That is a flower-book etymology rather than a philologist's, so read it as one author's account.

In the language of flowers the mignonette meant that your qualities surpass your charms [2]. Its large cousin dyer's weed, *Reseda luteola*, stood for relief [2]. Paterson's entry for reseda ends by calling the color "also called *Reseda luteola*", which is the dyer's weed and not the mignonette [1][2]. The two plants share a genus, and the color word comes from the sweet-scented one, so the dictionary runs them together.

The overlap is old. Pastoureau's French edition calls weld a kind of *réséda*, and his English edition says weld is also called reseda [3][4].

sections.title: Which green is reseda
sections.body:
Our swatch, #9F9F52, comes from a single source, the Maerz and Paul color dictionary of 1930, plate 22 K 1, which records *Reseda* as first used in 1875 [5]. The same plate carries *Bladder Green*, first recorded in 1830, and *Mignonette*, first recorded in 1885 [5]. The swatch is a yellowish olive green rather than the grey-green Paterson describes [1][5]. Its nearest familiar name is [[moss]], 6 units away, and its closest neighbor in our palette is [[lettuce-green]] [5].

Other standards disagree about the word. Ridgway's 1912 atlas has a separate Mignonette Green on plate XXXI [6]. RAL's Reseda Green, RAL 6011, sits in our library as a near-duplicate of [[civette-green]], a grey-green about 17 units from this swatch [5]. So the word runs from yellow-olive to grey-green depending on whose chart you open.

sections.title: Weld, the reseda that dyed
sections.body:
Weld, *Reseda luteola*, is a tall herbaceous plant whose whole body carries a yellow dye, mainly the flavonoid luteolin [4][8]. Pastoureau reports weld seeds from lakeside settlements on Swiss lakes dated to 3000 or 4000 BCE, and cannot prove they were harvested for dye [9]. He adds that weld was the main yellow dye plant in Europe from antiquity until the nineteenth century [9]. The Pigment Compendium calls it the most universally used yellow dye in medieval Europe before quercitron became available [8].

The Romans called weld *lutum* and gave its dyers a guild of their own, the luteolarii, among the eleven trades of a decree on dyers [10]. Weld gave very solid yellows, less bright and less orange than saffron, and it needed a strong mordant, generally tartar or alum [10]. Chaucer named madder, weld and woad as the three staples of the dyeing industry [14].

Dyers prized it for silk. Paterson says weld was used particularly for silk, and that the plant, also called dyer's rocket, grows fast to about six feet [11]. Coles calls it the oldest European dye plant, cultivated commercially well into the twentieth century [12].

sections.title: Weld and woad make green
sections.body:
Weld's second career was as the yellow half of green. Vitruvius, in the first century BCE, says that people who cannot afford malachite steep blue dye in weld to get a brilliant green, which he calls dyer's green [8]. Coptic tunics used the same pairing, indigo with yellow weld for green [13]. In medieval Britain the greens called Saxon, Lincoln and Kendal were made from woad with weld or dyer's broom [15].

Pastoureau reads the practice in a lawsuit. In January 1386 the Nuremberg dyer Hans Töllner, licensed only for blue and black, was found with yellow vats, fined and exiled, and Pastoureau infers that he was making green by dipping woad blue into weld [16]. Guild rules usually forbade the two-step dyeing, because blue dyers and yellow dyers were licensed apart [16]. Pastoureau notes that a Venetian dyeing manual of 1540 is the first to describe the method in print, though he calls the method very old [16].

The famous Lincoln green was a showy, expensive cloth rather than camouflage, Finlay argues [17]. It needed two vats, woad blue over weld yellow [17].

sections.title: Why old forests are blue
sections.body:
Weld is a fugitive yellow. In medieval and Renaissance tapestries the yellow faded first, so green foliage reverted to blue, a process Balfour-Paul calls preferential fading, or "blue disease" [18]. Finlay says the same of weld: after seven hundred years on castle walls, tapestry forests tend to be misty blue [17]. The blue that remains is the woad, which stays blue as it pales, and the Bayeux tapestry still shows its woad blue [18].

Where to look: in an old tapestry, a blue tree is often a green tree whose weld has gone.

sections.title: Weld as a paint
sections.body:
Painters used weld too. Cennini, about 1400, described the yellow lake made from weld, which he called *arzica*, as an artificial color for miniature painting [8]. Ball reports that Cennino was not enthusiastic, finding it little used, thin in color and apt to fade in the open [19]. The lake is a dye turned into a pigment: the whole dried plant is stewed in a weak alum solution and the color is precipitated out [8][12]. Books differ on the precipitant. The Compendium names calcium sulfate, eggshell or lead white, and Coles names potash [8][12]. Coles adds that the lake is translucent, which suits glazing [12].

In the seventeenth century a yellow called *pink* was an extract of weld, broom or unripe buckthorn berries fixed on chalk or a similar white [19]. Ball says the word named the method of making, not a color [19]. Pastoureau reports that analysis found weld lake and massicot in the dress of Baldovinetti's *Portrait of a Woman in Yellow*, about 1465, which helped move the picture's attribution from Piero della Francesca to Baldovinetti [20].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, 217 hold colors within six units of this swatch over at least five per cent of the canvas, 0.9 per cent [21]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a hue, not a pigment test, and says nothing about mignonette or weld [21].

The color arrives late. None of the 1,388 paintings dated 1100 to 1499 hold it, and the first match at this threshold is Luini's [[painting:nga-12158|Procris and the Unicorn]] of about 1520, at 22 per cent of the canvas [21]. It then grows: 1.3 per cent of paintings in the 1800s and 2.7 per cent in the 1900s, 3.0 times the archive rate [21].

The painter most tied to it is [[painter:georges-seurat|Seurat]], who holds it in 11 of his 41 works here, 29 times the archive rate; [[painter:vincent-van-gogh|Van Gogh]] holds it in 5 of 49 [21]. The widest covers are a Mewar court painting of about 1680, [[painting:cma-314442|The Elephant of Maharana Jai Singh]], at 67 per cent, and Soutine's 1916 [[painting:commons-Q21722881|Self-Portrait]], at 47 per cent [21]. Indian painting carries the color 3.2 times as often as the average, 21 of 721 works [21].

Its usual company on a canvas is [[moss]] at 13 times chance, [[khaki]] at 12.6 times and [[olive]] at 7.0 times [21].
